title: Tax-Advantaged Accounts
description: Traditional or Roth, the 2026 limits, and the penalty on an early traditional withdrawal.
wolfLine: The match is free pay. The early withdrawal is a penalty.

traditional-ira.definition: An individual retirement account. A contribution can be deductible now, and withdrawals in retirement are usually taxed.
traditional-ira.example: A $2,000 deductible contribution in the 12% bracket saves $240 this year.

roth-ira.definition: An individual retirement account you fund with money that has already been taxed. Qualified withdrawals later are tax-free.
roth-ira.example: A $2,000 Roth contribution saves $0 of tax this year. The qualified withdrawals are the point.

lessons.title: Now or Later
lessons.summary: Same $2,000. The tax moves to a different year.

steps.context: A [[traditional IRA]] can be a deduction now. A [[Roth IRA]] is funded after tax. Qualified Roth withdrawals later are tax-free. This is the trade, not a personal plan.

steps.prompt: A $2,000 deductible traditional contribution is in the 12% bracket. How much tax does it save this year?

steps.prompt: Which page buys a deduction this year?
why: The $240 is tax saved this year.
The Roth contribution is not deductible.
Only the traditional page is a deduction.
steps.explain: The traditional page saves $240 now. The Roth page already paid that $240.

steps.prompt: Which page is built so a qualified withdrawal later is tax-free?
choices: Neither. Both are taxed again later
steps.explain: That is the Roth bargain. Traditional withdrawals are usually taxed later.

steps.prompt: The Roth contribution in this pair saves $240 of tax this year.
steps.explain: The $240 on the Roth page is tax already paid. The traditional page is the one that saves it.

steps.prompt: Qualified Roth withdrawals are ___.
steps.explain: Tax-free, when they are qualified. That is why you paid tax on the way in.

lessons.title: 2026 Limits
lessons.summary: The employee deferral and the IRA cap are different numbers.

steps.title: Label the year
steps.body:
For 2026, the employee [[401(k)|401k]] deferral limit is **$24,500**. The catch-up at age 50 is **$8,000**, so **$32,500**. At ages 60, 61, 62, and 63 the catch-up is **$11,250**, so **$35,750**.

The IRA limit, traditional and Roth combined, is **$7,500**, plus **$1,100** at age 50, so **$8,600**. The employer match is not part of the $24,500.

steps.prompt: What is the 2026 employee 401(k) deferral limit, before any catch-up?
At age 50, the 401(k) catch-up is $8,000. What is the total you can defer?
What is the 2026 IRA limit before the age-50 catch-up?
steps.explain: $7,500, shared by traditional and Roth contributions.

steps.prompt: At age 50, the IRA catch-up is $1,100. What is the total IRA limit?

lessons.title: The HSA’s Three Tax Breaks
lessons.summary: In, growth, and qualified money out.

steps.title: Already on the path
steps.body:
An [[HSA|health-savings-account]] can be pre-tax or deductible on the way in, can grow without a yearly tax, and can come out tax-free for qualified medical costs.

For 2026 the contribution limit is **$4,400** with self-only coverage and **$8,750** with family coverage, plus **$1,000** at age 55. You need a qualifying health plan. This is the same HSA you already met.

steps.prompt: What is the 2026 HSA limit for self-only coverage, before the age-55 catch-up?
What is the 2026 family HSA limit, before that catch-up?
Age 55 adds $1,000. What is the self-only total then?
An HSA is the same account as a 529 plan.
steps.explain: An HSA is for qualified medical costs. A 529 is for education.

lessons.title: A 529, Again
lessons.summary: Education money. Not a promised return.

steps.title: The tax piece
steps.body:
A [[529 plan]] is still the education account from the family unit. Qualified withdrawals are tax-free at the federal level. The investments inside can fall.

**$150** a month is **$1,800** a year of contributions. That is the part you choose. The balance later is not a rate this course will invent.

steps.prompt: What is $150 a month for a year?
What is the federal tax rule this lesson will stand behind?
choices: The balance rises by a set percent
Contributions are always deductible on the federal return
steps.explain: The qualified withdrawal is the rule. A federal deduction for the contribution is not the promise.

steps.prompt: A 529 contribution and an HSA contribution share one 2026 limit.
steps.explain: They are different accounts with different limits.

steps.prompt: A qualified 529 withdrawal for education is federally ___.
steps.explain: Tax-free when it is qualified. The investment result is separate.

lessons.title: Which Account First
lessons.summary: A common sketch. Not an order the IRS requires.

steps.title: Match, then the expensive debt, then the HSA
steps.body:
A common order: take the full employer match, pay high-interest debt, fund an [[HSA|health-savings-account]] if you qualify, then an IRA or more of the [[401(k)|401k]].

The match is a 100% return on the dollars it matches. Skipping it to buy a taxable fund first gives away that match. This is a sketch, not a rule for every household.

steps.prompt: Put this common sketch in order.
items: Fund an HSA if you qualify
Add an IRA or more of the 401(k)
steps.explain: The match is first because it is extra pay. High-interest debt and a qualifying HSA come before the extra retirement dollars.

steps.prompt: The employer matches dollar for dollar up to a cap. What is the cost of not contributing enough to get the full match?
choices: The IRS fines you the same amount
steps.explain: The match is pay you do not receive. It is not a fine.

steps.prompt: This order is required by the tax code.
steps.explain: It is a common sketch. A household with no match, or no qualifying health plan, starts in a different place.

steps.prompt: The first stop in this sketch is the employer ___.
steps.explain: Match. It is the piece of pay that depends on your contribution.

lessons.title: Early Withdrawals
lessons.summary: Usually a 10% penalty, plus the tax.

steps.title: Before 59½
steps.body:
Money taken from a [[traditional IRA]] or a 401(k) before age **59½** is usually hit with a **10%** penalty, and it is usually taxed as income. Exceptions exist. This lesson stays with the common case.

A **$1,000** early traditional withdrawal has a **$100** penalty. The **$1,000** is also income. Roth contributions, not the earnings, can usually come out without tax or penalty. Do not treat the whole Roth account that way.

steps.prompt: What is the 10% penalty on a $1,000 early traditional withdrawal?
The $1,000 is also taxed in the 12% bracket. How much income tax does that add, on top of the penalty?
steps.explain: $1,000 × 0.12 = $120. The penalty is separate.

steps.prompt: What do the $100 penalty and the $120 of income tax cost together?
steps.explain: $100 + $120 = $220. You also no longer have the $1,000 invested.

steps.prompt: Roth contributions and Roth earnings follow the exact same early-withdrawal rule.
steps.explain: Contributions can usually come out. Earnings have their own rules. The traditional withdrawal is the one with the usual 10% penalty.

lessons.title: The Withdrawal on the Statement
lessons.summary: The deferral is the plan. The withdrawal is the leak.

steps.title: Three lines
steps.body:
The **$4,000** deferral is money going in. The **$1,000** line is an early withdrawal from a [[traditional IRA]]. The **$100** is the 10% penalty.

The deferral is not the problem.

steps.prompt: Which line is the early withdrawal?
steps.explain: The $1,000 traditional IRA withdrawal is the line. The penalty is the cost of that line, not a second withdrawal.

steps.prompt: What is 10% of that $1,000 withdrawal?
Which line is the useful one?
steps.explain: The deferral is the contribution. The other two are the leak and its cost.

steps.prompt: The penalty replaces the income tax on the withdrawal.
steps.explain: The $100 is the penalty. The $1,000 is usually income as well.

lessons.title: Kim’s $6,000
lessons.summary: The IRA cap is $7,500. She is assigning less than that.

story.title: Kim splits $6,000
story.body:
Kim is 36 and a nurse. She has **$6,000** to assign this year, after she has already taken her employer match. She is in the 12% bracket.

A **$2,000** [[traditional IRA]] deduction would save **$240**. She still wants at least **$2,000** in a [[Roth IRA]], because she wants qualified withdrawals later to be tax-free. The 2026 IRA limit is **$7,500**, so **$6,000** fits inside it if every IRA dollar stays at or under that cap.

She assigns the whole $6,000. The Roth gets at least $2,000. The rest can be a traditional IRA or a taxable brokerage account.

steps.prompt: Assign $6,000. The Roth IRA needs at least $2,000. Assign every dollar.
steps.explain: The Roth gets at least $2,000. All $6,000 is assigned, and $6,000 is under the 2026 IRA limit of $7,500.

steps.prompt: If all $6,000 went into IRAs, how much of the $7,500 limit would be left?
A $2,000 traditional deduction in her 12% bracket saves how much this year?
Why can she put the whole $6,000 into IRAs and still be inside the 2026 limit?
choices: Roth dollars do not count toward the IRA limit
steps.explain: Traditional and Roth share the $7,500 limit. $6,000 fits.

steps.prompt: Her employer match is part of the $24,500 employee deferral limit.
steps.explain: The $24,500 is what she defers from her pay. The match is the employer’s money, under a different cap.

Qualified Roth withdrawals are taxed a second time.
